reason: The final fragment is a phrase Augustine quotes from Julian about human nature. The Virgil and Sirach material belongs to Augustine’s response.
The second excerpt’s pronouns are adapted from Augustine’s report. The final claim repeats the position previously recovered in Against Julian 5.9.36.
The long quotation about birth and rebirth is Augustine’s Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.19.21. Augustine’s Johannine countertexts are excluded.
Augustine-only exposition of Johannine uses of ‘world’; no Julian excerpt.
Augustine’s conditional challenge and exposition; the proposed denial by Julian is hypothetical rather than a preserved claim.
Julian is describing baptismal benefits to infants. Augustine’s initial extracts from his own book and his Mark 16:16 objection are excluded.
Augustine-only exposition of Romans 6; no distinct Julian wording.
The first claim is explicitly recalled from Julian’s first book. Augustine’s constructed answer about Christ dying for sinners and nonsinners is not treated as an additional literal quotation.
Augustine’s continuous exposition of Romans 5, not Julian’s text.
Augustine’s continuous biblical argument, including hypothetical responses; no bounded Julian fragment.
Augustine says Julian omitted his qualification ‘not easily.’ The record preserves the disputed characterization, not an endorsement of its accuracy.
Augustine-only criticism of Julian’s appeal to what can be sensed; no distinct recoverable excerpt.
Augustine’s own Virgil citation and Romans 6 exposition; no Julian quotation.
Augustine’s own argument and biblical citations throughout.
Julian applies this to Augustine’s olive-tree analogy. Paul’s seed analogy is Augustine’s countertext, excluded.

These ancient zoological claims are preserved as Julian’s cited examples, not endorsed as modern biology. Augustine repeats the last two definitions and supplies counterexamples; repetitions and counterexamples are excluded.
Augustine also restates Julian’s point as the incomprehensibility of God’s works. Ecclesiastes 11:5 is Augustine’s supporting quotation, not explicitly Julian’s.
Augustine compares this to an earlier Pelagian statement; that separate Pelagius quotation and Augustine’s circumcision exposition are excluded.
Entire source section is a bracketed Augustine argument introducing a hypothetical objection, not a preserved Julian quotation.
The definition repeats 6.7.18. Augustine’s ensuing figurative examples, foreskin discussion, and Bible quotations are his own.
Augustine’s olive/circumcision argument and imagined infant’s speech; not Julian’s text.
The last excerpt contains an echo of Virgil, Aeneid 12.109, explicitly linked to Julian’s manner of speaking. Pronouns in the first two charges are adapted from Augustine’s report.

The first phrase is Julian’s dismissive term for artisans. The list reconstructs the allegations Augustine expressly denies; his inserted qualification ‘except toward unlawful acts’ is not attributed to Julian.
Three separated questions. Augustine’s 2 Corinthians 5:14 response is excluded.
Julian’s allegation about the God implied by Augustine’s teaching on infants, not Julian’s own description of God. Augustine repeats the allegation while disputing it.
A hostile characterization of Augustine’s position, which Augustine rejects. ‘Washed’ refers to baptism; Augustine expressly objects to Julian’s choice of this word instead of ‘reborn’ or ‘baptized.’
Augustine expressly says they do not regard baptism as superfluous. The preceding hypothetical argument and following biblical counterarguments are his own.
Two claims from Julian’s list of matters the Christian faith does not doubt. Augustine’s qualifications and counterexamples are excluded.
The wording preserves the Latin biblical text Julian cites. Augustine’s questions about its application to infants and his other biblical citations are excluded.
Two separated statements; the phrase defining innocence is explicitly quoted as Julian’s addition.
Julian’s demand is preserved within Augustine’s indirect quotation. Augustine’s reply about infants troubled by unclean spirits is excluded.

Repeated argument: Augustine points back to Against Julian 3.3.8–9. The language about having deserved neither good nor evil recalls Romans 9:11; Augustine’s subsequent use of Romans 9:22–23 is his own.
Julian proposes a sense for ‘by nature’; Augustine argues against it from the established Latin translations. ‘Truly’ renders prorsus, with the force ‘altogether’ or ‘really.’

The first sentence connects two explicitly quoted scraps using Augustine’s report. The second is a disputed characterization of Augustine’s view. Augustine’s imagined reply and his further quotation from Cicero, Against Catiline 2, are excluded.

Julian alleges that Augustine teaches this; Augustine explicitly denies it. The earlier ‘What times! What morals!’ repeats 6.11.34. The other quotation from Cicero and 1 Peter 3:9 belong to Augustine’s response.
The sentence is Augustine’s formulation of the view Julian attacks; Augustine denies holding it. It is therefore presented as a reported accusation, not a verbatim statement of Julian’s own doctrine.
No direct wording of Julian’s accusation is retained here. Augustine’s account of Zosimus, Innocent, and Caelestius is his rebuttal.
Only ‘God’s vengeance’ is directly quoted. Augustine challenges Julian’s account of divine action and contrasts an earlier dispute involving Damasus and Ursicinus.
Augustine preserves this in indirect quotation and denies the claim. His ensuing autobiographical explanation and biblical references are excluded.

Julian attributes these positions to Augustine; Augustine denies them. Julian had quoted Augustine’s On Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.17.19–1.18.20, including Luke 20:34, 2 Corinthians 4:16, 1 Corinthians 3:16, and Romans 8:23. That long Augustine passage is not a surviving work of Julian and is identified here rather than reproduced as his prose.

The first statement explains Galatians 5:17. The second is a short quoted claim within Augustine’s objection from Colossians 3:5. Augustine’s other biblical quotations and his account of the eunuch Calligonus are excluded.
Augustine’s continuing explanation of baptism, the temple, and desire; no distinct recoverable Julian quotation or report.
The disputed claim is framed by Augustine as Julian’s objection to his theology. God’s temple recalls 1 Corinthians 6:19; birth from God recalls John 1:13. Augustine’s lengthy response is excluded.

The first and last statements are allegations about Augustine’s teaching, which he rejects. ‘Supposedly’ translates the repeated quasi, playing on the Epicurean ‘something like a body.’ The source notes identify the Epicurean comparison with Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 3.3. Augustine’s own prayers and biblical arguments are excluded.

Julian is explaining Romans 8:23–24. The last clause echoes Romans 2:6 (also Matthew 16:27; Psalm 62:12, LXX/Vulgate 61:13). ‘Sifts’ renders expurget: the contrast is between forgiving sin and assessing each person’s deserts. Augustine’s Matthew 12:32 and Luke 23:42 counterarguments are excluded.

Julian’s description of the blessed resurrection is interrupted by Augustine’s response; the separated portions are reunited. Bruising and subjecting the body recalls 1 Corinthians 9:27; cheeks and back offered to blows recall Isaiah 50:6; strength from weakness recalls Hebrews 11:34. The phrase felicem impudentiam is unusual: literally ‘blessed/happy shamelessness,’ apparently fearless disregard for the shame of insults. Augustine’s suggested addition about chastity is not Julian’s text.
The last phrases partly repeat 6.15.46. Augustine’s use of James 1:14–15 and Romans 8:23 is his own argument, not a Julian citation here.
Augustine’s continued argument about desire, death, and baptism, with his own biblical citations; no distinct Julian fragment.

Augustine abbreviates the list in 1 Corinthians 6:9–10 with ‘and the rest’; the first paragraph translates only its surviving opening and conclusion, not the intervening unquoted items. His further biblical counterarguments are excluded.
Augustine refers to the earlier discussion at Against Julian 4.15.76. His polemical comparison with the monster Scylla and his claims about desire are not Julian’s language.

The disputed wording is Augustine’s On Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.25.28. The final phrase is explicitly attributed to Julian’s party in reference to infants. Augustine’s application of it to sexual desire as a ‘holy daughter of God’ is his own parody and is excluded.

Augustine develops hypothetical consequences if everything present in a baptized person must itself be baptized. No distinct Julian wording survives; his claim that Julian allows no evil to remain after baptism repeats the position already preserved.
Augustine preserves the accusation in indirect quotation and denies ever calling lust a substance. His discussion of other philosophers is his own explanation.

A technical distinction in the Aristotelian classification of qualities. ‘Passing state’ renders affectio; ‘enduring quality of feeling’ renders affectionalis qualitas. The latter concerns persistent dispositions, not simply emotions. Augustine’s explanatory examples and Romans 7 quotations are excluded.
Augustine’s account of inherited vice, habit, baptism, and propagation, without a distinct Julian fragment.
The introductory image is preserved as a quoted phrase embedded in Augustine’s report; the return to Scripture follows that report. Augustine’s objections and biblical counterarguments are excluded.
The verse under discussion is recoverable, but Julian’s particular explanation is not restated here. The interpretation of illnesses as continuing inner struggles is Augustine’s.

Julian was challenging Augustine’s On Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.23.26, on the devil’s wound and fruit from its own shrub. The allegation is disputed; Augustine’s tree-and-fruit explanation from Matthew 7:17 is his rebuttal.
Augustine’s own account of creation, grace, and election, with no distinct Julian fragment.

Julian challenges the logical reversal in Augustine’s claim that sins can pass in act but remain in guilt, while desire can remain in act but pass in guilt (On Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.26.29). ‘Reversed’ renders reciprocationem, concerning whether the contrasted terms may exchange positions in the argument. Augustine quotes the objection twice with different wording; both forms are retained. His Luke 13:32 interpretation is excluded.
Julian’s counterexample to Augustine’s claim that desire remains while its guilt is removed. Augustine accepts the account of idol sacrifice but rejects the proposed analogy.
Augustine’s subsequent account of where guilt remains, and his appeal to Colossians 2:14, are his own response.
Augustine preserves Julian’s argument in indirect quotation after citing his own On Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.23.26. The argument concerns responsibility for one’s own voluntary faults.

A technical argument from Aristotelian categories against Augustine’s use of ‘lesser’ and ‘greater’ for humanity and angelic nature. The distinction between receiving contraries and having a contrary is preserved as the Latin states it; Augustine rejects its relevance.
Julian argues against what he takes to follow from Augustine’s position. Augustine’s agricultural counterexample and scriptural citations are excluded.

A collection of Julian’s claims, repeated from Against Julian 1.8.41; 1.9.42–44; and 5.16.59,64. Augustine says Julian had also quoted Mani to compare with Augustine, but does not reproduce those Mani excerpts here.

Julian’s taunt about Augustine’s former religion; the fuller’s cleansing herb recalls Malachi 3:2. Augustine’s preceding Cicero quotation and hypothetical Manichean argument are his own, not Julian excerpts.

Julian quoted Augustine’s On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins 1.28.56, contrasting Eve’s belief in the serpent with the Virgin’s belief in the angel. Augustine denies the sexual interpretation; his following 2 Corinthians 11:3 and 1 Corinthians 15:33 arguments are excluded.

The opening claim is reconstructed from Augustine’s quoted second-person report. Basil and John’s passages are discussed earlier in Against Julian 1.5–6, and ‘a conspiracy of lost men’ repeats 1.7. The popular reaction is Julian’s characterization of his opponents’ case, not the editor’s verdict.

The Scripture gives the endpoints of the passage under dispute, not the whole passage verbatim. The report about the saints’ struggle refers back to Against Julian 3.21. Augustine’s account of his change of interpretation and his other citations are excluded.
The second paragraph is Julian’s disputed characterization of Augustine’s interpretation, not an accusation that Paul actually visited prostitutes. Augustine’s Romans 7:20 response is excluded.

Julian’s proposed speaker in Romans 7 is presented as a reported interpretation, with the final reason quoted. Augustine rejects this reading; his further description of Julian’s theory of grace is polemical commentary and is not reproduced as a direct fragment.
Augustine expressly says Julian quoted Romans 7:12–13. The many surrounding Romans quotations are Augustine’s answer, not additional Julian citations in this section.
Augustine continues his own distinction between bodily nature and evil desires; no distinct Julian fragment.

The argument turns on the Latin in quo, which can be read ‘in whom’ or ‘in which/by what’ according to context. Julian proposes a causal sense. The explanatory second paragraph is Augustine’s report; his Cain and homicide counterexamples are excluded.

Augustine explicitly identifies these as Julian’s supporting texts. They illustrate the proposed causal sense of ‘in/by’: ‘because of what’ or ‘because of this word.’ The psalm repeats the text discussed in 6.24.75. Augustine’s objections about imitation are excluded.

Julian supplies wording he thinks Paul would have used if Romans 5:12 concerned inherited sin. These are Julian’s hypothetical formulations, not quotations of Scripture. Augustine’s competing hypothetical formulations are excluded.
A chain of biblical testimony entirely supplied by Augustine in support of divine wrath and original sin. None is attributed to Julian here.
Augustine’s continuing exposition of Romans 5 and his argument against imitation. No distinct Julian fragment; the source note ‘1 John 3:36’ is an error for John 3:36 in Augustine’s own citation.
The first sentence is a short directly quoted explanation; the second states its setting. Augustine’s examples from Abraham and his other biblical citations are excluded.

Augustine repeats Julian’s distinction between many and all, already preserved at 6.24.80, then develops his own account of its consequences. ‘But more easily through Christ’ is introduced as an imagined answer, not quoted Julian text.

Augustine identifies this as Julian’s final and supposedly strongest prophetic proof. The wording is Augustine’s summary of the passage Julian invokes, not an uninterrupted direct biblical quotation. Verse 20 is added because it supplies the father-and-son clause, beyond the source note’s Ezekiel 18:2–4. The subsequent biblical countertexts all belong to Augustine.

The conclusion reports Julian’s claims rather than preserving an extended direct quotation. Augustine’s imagined speeches by biblical figures, Cyprian, and Ambrose are his own counterargument and are excluded.
